items.stem: Which of the following is the main assumption of the simple two-sector circular flow model?
options: Households save part of their income
Households spend all their income and there is no government or foreign trade
items.answer: Households spend all their income and there is no government or foreign trade
items.markingKey: D. In the closed model all income is spent, so the flow stays constant.

items.stem: Hana writes: "Profit is not part of the circular flow because firms keep it." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Profit is the reward to entrepreneurship and is paid to the households who own firms, so it is part of factor income.
items.markingKey: Profit is the reward to entrepreneurship and is paid to the households who own firms, so it is part of factor income. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "In the circular flow, firms own the factors of production." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Households own the factors of production and sell their services to firms in factor markets.
items.markingKey: Households own the factors of production and sell their services to firms in factor markets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain what happens to the circular flow if households in a two-sector economy suddenly cut their spending by 10%.
items.answer: Firms' revenues fall by 10%, so they cut output and pay less in factor incomes; household incomes fall, which reduces spending further – the flow shrinks.
items.markingKey: Firms' revenues fall by 10%, so they cut output and pay less in factor incomes; household incomes fall, which reduces spending further – the flow shrinks.

items.stem: A student claims that Profit is not part of the circular flow because firms keep it. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Profit is the reward to entrepreneurship and is paid to the households who own firms, so it is part of factor income.
items.markingKey: Profit is the reward to entrepreneurship and is paid to the households who own firms, so it is part of factor income. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using an appropriate diagram, explain the simple two-sector circular flow of income between households and firms.
items.answer: Diagram: two boxes, households and firms. Inner loop (real flows): factors of production from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households. Outer loop (money flows): factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms. With no leakages or injections income = output = expenditure and the flow is constant.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: two boxes, households and firms. Inner loop (real flows): factors of production from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households. Outer loop (money flows): factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms. With no leakages or injections income = output = expenditure and the flow is constant. Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Households, rather than firms, are the most important economic agents in the circular flow."
items.answer: Neither is more important: the model's central message is the interdependence of households and firms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: households own all factors of production; consumption is the largest component of spending. Arguments against: firms organise production and create income; the two are interdependent: neither can function alone. Supported judgement: Neither is more important: the model's central message is the interdependence of households and firms.

items.stem: Explain, with reference to the circular flow of income, why the three methods of measuring national income should give the same result.
items.answer: Output method values goods produced; income method adds factor incomes paid by firms; expenditure method adds spending on output. In the circular flow, the value of output is paid as incomes, which are spent on output, so all three are equal (subject to statistical discrepancies).
items.markingKey: Output method values goods produced; income method adds factor incomes paid by firms; expenditure method adds spending on output. In the circular flow, the value of output is paid as incomes, which are spent on output, so all three are equal (subject to statistical discrepancies).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An economic agent that owns the factors of production and consumes goods and services"?
items.answer: household
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of household.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "circular flow of income".
items.answer: A model showing the flows of money and real resources between households and firms (and, in the full model, government, financial and foreign sectors)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a model showing the flows of money and real resources between households and firms (and, in the full model, government, financial and foreign sectors). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why in the simple circular flow model the value of output equals the value of income and of expenditure.
items.answer: Firms' revenue from selling output is paid out as factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit), and households spend all income on firms' output, so output = income = expenditure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Firms' revenue from selling output is paid out as factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit), and households spend all income on firms' output, so output = income = expenditure. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the real flow and the money flow.
items.answer: The money flow is the payments (incomes and spending); the real flow is the goods, services and factors of production exchanged for those payments, moving in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: The money flow is the payments (incomes and spending); the real flow is the goods, services and factors of production exchanged for those payments, moving in the opposite direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In Country K households receive wages of $519bn, rent of $76bn, interest of $58bn and profits of $74bn. Assuming a simple two-sector circular flow, calculate total household spending.
items.markingKey: All income is spent: 519 + 76 + 58 + 74 = $727bn. [1] working [1] answer.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the fall in tourist spending in Thailand in 2020 shows the circular flow of income.
items.answer: International tourist arrivals fell from almost 40 million in 2019 to under 7 million in 2020. Less spending on hotels and restaurants reduced firms' revenues, so they cut wages and jobs; households' incomes fell, reducing their own spending – the flow of income shrank.
items.markingKey: Context (International tourist arrivals fell from almost 40 million in 2019 to under 7 million in 2020.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Less spending on hotels and restaurants reduced firms' revenues, so they cut wages and jobs; households' incomes fell, reducing their own spending – the flow of income shrank. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the circular flow of income.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the circular flow model is too simple to explain how a real economy works?
items.answer: The simple model is a starting point; extended with leakages and injections it is the basis of national income accounting and macroeconomic analysis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ignores prices and inflation; assumes all income is spent in the simple model; does not show distribution of income. Arguments against: shows interdependence clearly; explains why output = income = expenditure (basis of national accounts); can be extended with leakages and injections. Supported judgement: The simple model is a starting point; extended with leakages and injections it is the basis of national income accounting and macroeconomic analysis. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "injection"?
options: Spending that enters the circular flow and does not come from households' consumption: investment, government spending and exports
The part of household income that is not spent on consumption
Measuring national output as C + I + G + (X − M)
A market in which firms sell goods and services to households
items.answer: Spending that enters the circular flow and does not come from households' consumption: investment, government spending and exports
items.markingKey: A. "injection" is spending that enters the circular flow and does not come from households' consumption: investment, government spending and exports.

items.stem: "Taxes are an injection into the circular flow because the government spends them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Taxes are a leakage – they take income out of the flow; government spending is a separate injection, and the two need not be equal.
items.markingKey: Taxes are a leakage – they take income out of the flow; government spending is a separate injection, and the two need not be equal. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why saving is a leakage from the circular flow.
items.answer: Saving is income that households do not spend on domestic output; it is taken out of the flow of spending, so firms' revenues are lower unless the savings are lent and spent on investment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Saving is income that households do not spend on domestic output; it is taken out of the flow of spending, so firms' revenues are lower unless the savings are lent and spent on investment. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to remittances to the Philippines, explain how it illustrates injections into the circular flow from the foreign sector.
items.answer: Overseas Filipino workers sent home around $37 billion in 2023, about 9% of GDP. Remittances add to household incomes from abroad, increasing spending and the size of the domestic circular flow.
items.markingKey: Context (Overseas Filipino workers sent home around $37 billion in 2023, about 9% of GDP.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Remittances add to household incomes from abroad, increasing spending and the size of the domestic circular flow. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to injections into the circular flow from the foreign sector.

items.stem: In Freedonia, saving is $42bn, taxes $60bn, imports $78bn, investment $80bn, government spending $145bn and exports $50bn. Calculate total leakages and total injections, and state what will happen to national income.
items.answer: Leakages $180bn, injections $275bn; national income will rise (injections exceed leakages)
items.markingKey: Leakages = 42 + 60 + 78 = 180 [1]; injections = 80 + 145 + 50 = 275 [1]; income will rise (injections exceed leakages) [2].

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that a rise in household saving is always bad for an economy.
items.answer: Higher saving reduces demand in the short run, especially in a recession, but supports investment and long-run growth if the financial sector channels it effectively.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: saving is a leakage that reduces spending and can cause recession (paradox of thrift); lower consumption reduces firms' revenues. Arguments against: savings fund investment, which raises future productive capacity; households build buffers against shocks; higher saving can reduce reliance on foreign borrowing. Supported judgement: Higher saving reduces demand in the short run, especially in a recession, but supports investment and long-run growth if the financial sector channels it effectively.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Spending by firms on capital goods such as machinery, buildings and technology"?
items.answer: investment
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of investment.

items.stem: Explain why the size of the circular flow increases when injections exceed leakages.
items.answer: More spending enters the flow than leaves it, so firms' revenues rise; they expand output and pay more factor incomes, increasing national income until leakages rise to match injections.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: More spending enters the flow than leaves it, so firms' revenues rise; they expand output and pay more factor incomes, increasing national income until leakages rise to match injections. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why exports are an injection into the circular flow.
items.answer: Exports are spending by foreigners on domestic output; this money enters the domestic circular flow from outside, adding to firms' revenues and to incomes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Exports are spending by foreigners on domestic output; this money enters the domestic circular flow from outside, adding to firms' revenues and to incomes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the four-sector model and the two-sector model.
items.answer: The two-sector model includes only households and firms with no leakages or injections; the four-sector open model adds the financial, government and foreign sectors with saving/investment, taxes/government spending and imports/exports.
items.markingKey: The two-sector model includes only households and firms with no leakages or injections; the four-sector open model adds the financial, government and foreign sectors with saving/investment, taxes/government spending and imports/exports. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Imports are harmful to an economy because they are a leakage from the circular flow." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Imports are a leakage in the accounting sense, but they raise living standards and efficiency; what matters is the overall balance of leakages and injections.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: imports reduce spending on domestic output; can reduce domestic employment in import-competing industries. Arguments against: imports give consumers choice and lower prices; imported capital goods and inputs raise productivity; other countries' import spending is our export injection. items.stem: Explain the difference between equilibrium national income and full employment national income.
items.answer: Equilibrium is where leakages equal injections, so income is stable; this need not be at full employment – the economy may be in equilibrium with unemployment.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium is where leakages equal injections, so income is stable; this need not be at full employment – the economy may be in equilibrium with unemployment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Equilibrium national income means the economy has no unemployment." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Equilibrium only means income is not changing; it can occur at a level below full employment.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium only means income is not changing; it can occur at a level below full employment. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Germany's large current account surplus in the 2010s shows the link between leakages and injections in national income.
items.answer: Germany's exports exceeded imports by around 7-8% of GDP, while households saved a high share of income. High saving (leakage) was offset by a high level of net exports (injection), so (S − I) + (T − G) = (X − M) was positive.
items.markingKey: Context (Germany's exports exceeded imports by around 7-8% of GDP, while households saved a high share of income.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High saving (leakage) was offset by a high level of net exports (injection), so (S − I) + (T − G) = (X − M) was positive. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the link between leakages and injections in national income.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how equilibrium national income is restored after an increase in government spending, using the circular flow model.
items.answer: Diagram: four-sector circular flow; G (injection) rises, so injections > leakages; spending and incomes rise; as income rises, saving, taxes and imports rise; a new equilibrium is reached at a higher national income where S + T + M = I + G + X.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: four-sector circular flow; G (injection) rises, so injections > leakages; spending and incomes rise; as income rises, saving, taxes and imports rise; a new equilibrium is reached at a higher national income where S + T + M = I + G + X. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Using the circular flow, explain what happens to equilibrium national income if a fall in business confidence reduces investment by $15bn while all other injections are unchanged.
items.answer: Injections fall below leakages; firms' revenues fall, they cut output and incomes; as income falls, saving, taxes and imports fall until total leakages again equal the lower level of injections, at a lower equilibrium national income.
items.markingKey: Injections fall below leakages; firms' revenues fall, they cut output and incomes; as income falls, saving, taxes and imports fall until total leakages again equal the lower level of injections, at a lower equilibrium national income.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The total value of income earned by a country's factors of production in a year; equal in principle to output and expenditure"?
items.answer: national income
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of national income.

items.stem: Explain why the circular flow can be in equilibrium even if the government runs a budget deficit.
items.answer: Equilibrium requires total leakages to equal total injections; a deficit (G > T) can be offset by saving exceeding investment or imports exceeding exports.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Equilibrium requires total leakages to equal total injections; a deficit (G > T) can be offset by saving exceeding investment or imports exceeding exports. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between nominal GDP and real GDP.
items.answer: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so changes reflect changes in the quantity of output.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that a country that saves more than it invests must run a trade surplus.
items.answer: The identity links them, but excess private saving can be offset by a government deficit; the trade balance results from all sectoral balances together.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: from the identity (S − I) + (T − G) = X − M; examples: Germany, China. Arguments against: a government deficit can absorb excess private saving; the identity does not show causation; exchange rates and capital flows also adjust. Judgement: The identity links them, but excess private saving can be offset by a government deficit; the trade balance results from all sectoral balances together. items.answer: Only the totals must be equal: S + T + M = I + G + X. Individual pairs can be unbalanced as long as they offset each other.
items.markingKey: Only the totals must be equal: S + T + M = I + G + X. Individual pairs can be unbalanced as long as they offset each other. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the fall in tourist spending in Thailand in 2020 as an example, explain the circular flow of income.
items.answer: International tourist arrivals fell from almost 40 million in 2019 to under 7 million in 2020. Less spending on hotels and restaurants reduced firms' revenues, so they cut wages and jobs; households' incomes fell, reducing their own spending – the flow of income shrank.
items.markingKey: Context (International tourist arrivals fell from almost 40 million in 2019 to under 7 million in 2020.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Less spending on hotels and restaurants reduced firms' revenues, so they cut wages and jobs; households' incomes fell, reducing their own spending – the flow of income shrank. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the circular flow of income.

items.stem: Outline the likely effect on the circular flow of Germany's economy of a sharp fall in exports to China.
items.answer: Exports are an injection; a fall reduces spending on German output, so firms' revenues and incomes fall and the circular flow shrinks (unless other injections rise or leakages fall).
items.markingKey: Exports are an injection; a fall reduces spending on German output, so firms' revenues and incomes fall and the circular flow shrinks (unless other injections rise or leakages fall).

items.stem: An economy has S = $90bn, T = $120bn, M = $70bn, I = $80bn, G = $130bn and X = $70bn. Is the circular flow in equilibrium? Explain.
items.answer: Leakages = 280, injections = 280, so yes – total leakages equal total injections even though S > I and G > T.
items.markingKey: Leakages = 280, injections = 280, so yes – total leakages equal total injections even though S > I and G > T.

items.stem: Briefly describe the fall in tourist spending in Thailand in 2020 and explain what it reveals about the circular flow of income.
items.answer: International tourist arrivals fell from almost 40 million in 2019 to under 7 million in 2020. Less spending on hotels and restaurants reduced firms' revenues, so they cut wages and jobs; households' incomes fell, reducing their own spending – the flow of income shrank.
items.markingKey: Context (International tourist arrivals fell from almost 40 million in 2019 to under 7 million in 2020.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using the four-sector circular flow model, explain how a government budget deficit can offset a rise in household saving.
items.answer: Higher saving increases leakages, which would shrink the flow; if government spending (injection) exceeds tax revenue (leakage), the deficit adds net injections that can offset the extra saving, keeping total injections equal to total leakages at the original level of income.
items.markingKey: Higher saving increases leakages, which would shrink the flow; if government spending (injection) exceeds tax revenue (leakage), the deficit adds net injections that can offset the extra saving, keeping total injections equal to total leakages at the original level of income.

items.stem: "A country that saves more than it invests must run a trade surplus." Discuss.
items.answer: The identity links them, but excess private saving can be offset by a government deficit; the trade balance results from all sectoral balances together.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: from the identity (S − I) + (T − G) = X − M; examples: Germany, China. Arguments against: a government deficit can absorb excess private saving; the identity does not show causation; exchange rates and capital flows also adjust. Supported judgement: The identity links them, but excess private saving can be offset by a government deficit; the trade balance results from all sectoral balances together. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that the circular flow model is too simple to explain how a real economy works.
items.answer: The simple model is a starting point; extended with leakages and injections it is the basis of national income accounting and macroeconomic analysis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ignores prices and inflation; assumes all income is spent in the simple model; does not show distribution of income. Arguments against: shows interdependence clearly; explains why output = income = expenditure (basis of national accounts); can be extended with leakages and injections. Judgement: The simple model is a starting point; extended with leakages and injections it is the basis of national income accounting and macroeconomic analysis. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that a rise in household saving is always bad for an economy.
items.answer: Higher saving reduces demand in the short run, especially in a recession, but supports investment and long-run growth if the financial sector channels it effectively.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: saving is a leakage that reduces spending and can cause recession (paradox of thrift); lower consumption reduces firms' revenues. Arguments against: savings fund investment, which raises future productive capacity; households build buffers against shocks; higher saving can reduce reliance on foreign borrowing. Judgement: Higher saving reduces demand in the short run, especially in a recession, but supports investment and long-run growth if the financial sector channels it effectively. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "factor market"?
options: The flow of goods, services and factors of production in the circular flow, opposite to the money flow
The part of household income that is not spent on consumption
A market in which households sell factors of production (e.g. labour) to firms in return for factor incomes
Measuring national output as C + I + G + (X − M)
items.answer: A market in which households sell factors of production (e.g. labour) to firms in return for factor incomes
items.markingKey: C. "factor market" is a market in which households sell factors of production (e.g. labour) to firms in return for factor incomes.

items.stem: Which sector of the circular flow is linked with saving and investment?
items.answer: The financial sector
items.markingKey: A. Banks and other financial institutions channel household savings to firms for investment.

items.stem: What is the expenditure method of calculating GDP?
items.answer: C + I + G + (X − M)
items.markingKey: C + I + G + (X − M). Imports are subtracted because they are spending on foreign output.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the circular flow shows that households and firms are interdependent.
items.answer: Households depend on firms for incomes and goods, while firms depend on households for factors of production and for spending; a fall in spending by households reduces firms' revenue and therefore incomes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Households depend on firms for incomes and goods, while firms depend on households for factors of production and for spending; a fall in spending by households reduces firms' revenue and therefore incomes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the four-sector model and the two-sector model.
items.answer: The two-sector model includes only households and firms with no leakages or injections; the four-sector open model adds the financial, government and foreign sectors with saving/investment, taxes/government spending and imports/exports.
items.markingKey: The two-sector model includes only households and firms with no leakages or injections; the four-sector open model adds the financial, government and foreign sectors with saving/investment, taxes/government spending and imports/exports. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why imports are subtracted in the expenditure method of measuring GDP.
items.answer: C, I and G include spending on imported goods; that spending creates income abroad, not domestically, so it must be removed to measure domestic output.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: C, I and G include spending on imported goods; that spending creates income abroad, not domestically, so it must be removed to measure domestic output. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the money flow and the real flow move in opposite directions.
items.answer: Money is paid in exchange for real goods and resources: households give labour to firms and receive wages, firms give goods to households and receive spending.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Money is paid in exchange for real goods and resources: households give labour to firms and receive wages, firms give goods to households and receive spending. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between leakages and injections.
items.answer: Leakages (saving, taxes, imports) take money out of the circular flow; injections (investment, government spending, exports) add spending to it.
items.markingKey: Leakages (saving, taxes, imports) take money out of the circular flow; injections (investment, government spending, exports) add spending to it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between real GDP and nominal GDP.
items.answer: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so changes reflect changes in the quantity of output.
items.markingKey: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so changes reflect changes in the quantity of output. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In Country K households receive wages of $535bn, rent of $56bn, interest of $67bn and profits of $190bn. Assuming a simple two-sector circular flow, calculate total household spending.
items.markingKey: All income is spent: 535 + 56 + 67 + 190 = $848bn. [1] working [1] answer.

items.stem: Classify each as a leakage or an injection for Kenya: (i) a German tourist on safari; (ii) a Kenyan family buying a Japanese car; (iii) the government building a new railway; (iv) a household putting money in a savings account.
items.answer: (i) injection (export); (ii) leakage (import); (iii) injection (government spending); (iv) leakage (saving).
items.markingKey: (i) injection (export); (ii) leakage (import); (iii) injection (government spending); (iv) leakage (saving).

items.stem: In equilibrium, Arcadia has investment $227bn, government spending $267bn, exports $236bn, taxes $273bn and imports $385bn. Calculate the level of saving consistent with equilibrium, and state the government budget balance.
items.answer: Saving = $72bn; budget balance = $6bn (surplus)

items.stem: A taxi driver in Bogotá earns wages from a ride-hailing company and spends them at a supermarket. Identify the flows in the circular flow model that this involves.
items.answer: Labour (real) flows from the household to a firm and wages (money) flow back – factor market; spending at the supermarket (money) flows to firms and groceries (real) flow to the household – product market.
items.markingKey: Labour (real) flows from the household to a firm and wages (money) flow back – factor market; spending at the supermarket (money) flows to firms and groceries (real) flow to the household – product market.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the circular flow of income in an open economy with a government sector, showing leakages and injections, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: households and firms with factor incomes and consumption flows; leakages leaving the flow: saving to the financial sector, taxes to government, imports to the foreign sector; injections entering the flow to firms: investment from the financial sector, government spending, exports. If injections > leakages, income rises; if leakages > injections, income falls.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: households and firms with factor incomes and consumption flows; leakages leaving the flow: saving to the financial sector, taxes to government, imports to the foreign sector; injections entering the flow to firms: investment from the financial sector, government spending, exports. If injections > leakages, income rises; if leakages > injections, income falls. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Briefly describe Germany's large current account surplus in the 2010s and explain what it reveals about the link between leakages and injections in national income.
items.answer: Germany's exports exceeded imports by around 7-8% of GDP, while households saved a high share of income. High saving (leakage) was offset by a high level of net exports (injection), so (S − I) + (T − G) = (X − M) was positive.
items.markingKey: Context (Germany's exports exceeded imports by around 7-8% of GDP, while households saved a high share of income.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High saving (leakage) was offset by a high level of net exports (injection), so (S − I) + (T − G) = (X − M) was positive. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the link between leakages and injections in national income.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the simple two-sector circular flow of income between households and firms.
items.answer: Diagram: two boxes, households and firms. Inner loop (real flows): factors of production from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households. Outer loop (money flows): factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms. With no leakages or injections income = output = expenditure and the flow is constant.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: two boxes, households and firms. Inner loop (real flows): factors of production from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households. Outer loop (money flows): factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms. With no leakages or injections income = output = expenditure and the flow is constant. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Imports are harmful to an economy because they are a leakage from the circular flow.
items.answer: Imports are a leakage in the accounting sense, but they raise living standards and efficiency; what matters is the overall balance of leakages and injections.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: imports reduce spending on domestic output; can reduce domestic employment in import-competing industries. Arguments against: imports give consumers choice and lower prices; imported capital goods and inputs raise productivity; other countries' import spending is our export injection. Supported judgement: Imports are a leakage in the accounting sense, but they raise living standards and efficiency; what matters is the overall balance of leakages and injections.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that equilibrium national income is always a desirable outcome for an economy.
items.answer: Equilibrium only means stability; it is desirable only if it is close to full employment and sustainable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stable income avoids inflationary or deflationary pressures. Arguments against: equilibrium may occur with high unemployment; equilibrium can hide large trade or budget imbalances. Judgement: Equilibrium only means stability; it is desirable only if it is close to full employment and sustainable. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that Households, rather than firms, are the most important economic agents in the circular flow.
items.answer: Neither is more important: the model's central message is the interdependence of households and firms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: households own all factors of production; consumption is the largest component of spending. Arguments against: firms organise production and create income; the two are interdependent: neither can function alone.
